name: Roman Aqueduct System
region: Mediterranean (Italy, Gaul, Iberia, North Africa, Levant)
summary: Gravity-fed water conveyance networks using arched bridges, siphons, and underground channels that supplied cities with clean water at scales not matched again until the 19th century.

claims.statement: Rome's 11 aqueducts delivered approximately 1 million cubic metres of water daily, serving a population of over 1 million
Aqueduct engineering was replicated across the empire with local adaptation — the Pont du Gard, Segovia, and Carthage systems each solved different terrain challenges
Some aqueduct segments remained in continuous use for over 1000 years; the Aqua Virgo (19 BCE) still feeds Rome's Trevi Fountain

evidence.source: Frontinus (c. 97 CE) De Aquaeductu Urbis Romae, translated by Herschel (1899)
Hodge (1992) Roman Aqueducts and Water Supply, Duckworth
Wilson (2008) Hydraulic Engineering and Water Supply, in Oleson (ed.) Oxford Handbook of Engineering and Technology in the Classical World
ACEA SpA maintenance records for Acqua Vergine (modern continuation of Aqua Virgo), Rome

notes: Low decentralisation (state-directed) but extraordinary longevity and replication. Paired with Indus plumbing, these two infrastructure entries show convergent evolution: different cultures solved water distribution independently with radically different governance models.
